en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga, 15.
Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesa (The Exposition of the Discourse on the Staff of Oneself)
Now he will explain the exposition of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta:
"Behold how fear has arisen from those who wield the rod against themselves,
and see the people in turmoil."
I shall proclaim the sense of spiritual urgency,
just as it was realized by me:
"Fear has arisen from the staff of self."
"Sticks": there are three sticks—the stick of body, the stick of speech, and the stick of mind.
Threefold bodily misconduct is the stick of body; fourfold verbal misconduct is the stick of speech; threefold mental misconduct is the stick of mind.
There are two kinds of fear:
fear pertaining to the present life and fear pertaining to future lives.
What is fear pertaining to the present life?
Here, someone engages in misconduct by body, engages in misconduct by speech, and engages in misconduct by mind; he kills living beings,
takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, ambushes highways,
commits adultery with another's wife, and speaks falsehoods.
Having seized him, they present him to the king, saying:
"Sire, this is a thief, a wrongdoer.
Inflict upon him whatever punishment you wish."
The king rebukes him.
Because of that rebuke, he gives rise to fear and experiences pain and mental distress.
From where does that fear, pain, and mental distress come to him?
Born from self-inflicted violence, arisen, produced, generated, and manifested—
even by this much the king is not satisfied.
The king then has him bound with either a wooden shackle, a rope bond, or an iron chain.
Or by binding with a tether, or by binding with a creeper, or by binding in confinement,
or by binding in enclosure, or by binding to a village, or by binding to a town, or by binding to a city, or by binding to a kingdom,
or by binding to a province, or even at the very least, he makes one subject to his command.
“You cannot depart from here.
Because of that bondage, he experiences pain and mental distress.
From where would such fear, pain, and mental distress come for him?
Whatever has arisen, come into being, been produced, fully manifested, and appeared from the stick of self-aggression—
even by this much the king was not satisfied.
The king had his wealth brought forth.
Whether it be a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand.
Because of the loss of wealth, he experiences suffering and mental distress.
From where does this fear, this suffering, and this mental distress come for him?
Born from self-inflicted violence, arisen, produced, brought forth, and manifested—
even by this much the king is not satisfied. Therefore,
the king has him subjected to various forms of torture.
They beat them with whips, they beat them with canes, they beat them with split bamboo;
they cut off their hands, they cut off their feet, they cut off both hands and feet; they cut off their ears, they cut off their noses, they cut off both ears and noses;
they subject them to the "spit-ox" torture, they shave them with a conch-shell shave, and they subject them to the "Rāhu’s mouth" torture.
He makes himself a garland of fire; he makes himself a torch carried in the hand; he makes himself a wreath of *eraka* grass; he makes himself a garment of bark; he makes himself a deer-skin;
he makes himself a hook-and-fisherman’s-net; he makes himself a coin-pattern; he makes himself a scraping with caustic lye;
he makes himself a revolving on a bar; he makes himself a pallet of straw; and he douses himself with boiling oil.
He has them devoured by dogs; he impales them alive on stakes; he cuts off their heads with swords.
Because of such judicial punishments, he experiences pain and mental distress.
From where would that fear, pain, and mental distress come to him?
It is born from the rod, produced, brought forth, generated, and manifested.
The king is the master of these four kinds of punishment.
On account of his own karma, with the breakup of the body after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower world, even in hell.
Then the wardens of hell inflict upon him a form of torture called the fivefold binding:
they drive a red-hot iron stake through one hand, they drive a red-hot iron stake through the other hand,
they drive a red-hot iron stake through one foot, they drive a red-hot iron stake through the other foot, and they drive a red-hot iron stake through the middle of his chest.
Thus, there he experiences painful, sharp, and bitter sensations;
yet he does not pass away until that evil kamma has been exhausted.
From where could such fear, suffering, and mental distress come for him?
Born from self-inflicted violence, arisen, produced, brought into being, and manifested—
this the wardens of hell, having laid him down, hack with axes.
There he experiences feelings that are painful, sharp, and bitter.
And he does not die as long as that evil kamma has not been exhausted.
Then the wardens of hell seize him, turn him upside down with his feet up and head down, and carve him with axes.
Then the wardens of hell yoke him to a chariot and drive him back and forth over a ground that is burning, blazing, and glowing... [and so on]...
Then the wardens of hell make him climb up and down a great mountain of glowing coals—blazing, fiercely burning, and aflame...
Then the wardens of hell seize him by his feet and head and cast him into a heated iron cauldron—blazing, fiercely burning, and aflame.
There he is cooked, boiling like froth.
Thus, being cooked there in the Boiling Foam, he goes up at one time, down at another, and across at another.
There he experiences painful, sharp, and bitter sensations;
yet he does not die as long as that evil kamma has not been exhausted.
From where does this fear, suffering, and mental distress come for him?
It is born from his own violence, arisen, produced, brought into being, and manifested.
Then the wardens of hell cast him into the great hell.
And that Great Hell has four corners and four gates,
divided into sections and precisely measured.
Its perimeter is bounded by an iron wall and covered over with iron;
its ground is made of iron.
Blazing and endowed with splendor,
it remains at all times pervading a hundred yojanas in every direction.
The torments of the stingy are terrible,
blazing with flames and difficult to approach;
they are forms that cause the hair to stand on end.
Terrifying, fearsome, and painful.
From the eastern wall,
a mass of flames has arisen.
While burning away evil deeds,
he is struck by the western wall; and against that western wall—
A mass of flame has arisen;
burning through evil deeds,
it is struck back by the eastern direction.
And from the northern wall,
a mass of flames arose,
burning away evil deeds.
It was struck by the sacrificial fee.
And from the wall of the sacrificial fee,
a pillar of flames arose.
While burning away evil deeds,
he encounters resistance from above;
and rising up from below, he is struck down.
A terrifying mass of flames,
burning evil deeds,
strikes against the covering.
Arising from burning charcoal,
a terrifying mass of flames burns away evil deeds.
It strikes against the ground like a glowing iron bowl— burning, heated, and aflame.
Thus one sees the Avīci hell below and above; there,
beings are exceedingly greedy.
Committing great crimes,
those whose actions are utterly evil are tormented and do not die.
The bodies of those inhabitants of hell are like the fire-god Jātavedas;
behold the power of their kamma!
It becomes neither ashes nor even soot.
They run toward the east,
and from there they run toward the west.
They run toward the north,
and from there they run toward the south;
to whichever direction they flee, [they run].
Each respective door is closed;
those beings seeking liberation have lost their hope of going forth.
Due to the condition of their karma, they are not able to emerge from there;
and as for their evil course of action—
"Much has been done that is yet unripened.
From where would fear, suffering, and mental distress come for such a person?
They have arisen, been produced, been generated, been brought forth, and become manifest from self-inflicted punishment.
From what are those sufferings of the hell realms, those sufferings of the animal realm, those sufferings of the sphere of hungry ghosts, and those sufferings of the human world born?
From what are they produced, from what are they generated, from what do they arise, from what do they come into being, and from what do they manifest?
They are born, produced, generated, arisen, and manifested from the rod of self.
"From self-stickiness fear has arisen;
behold the people in conflict.
"People" refers to kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, householders, renunciants, and gods.
“People! Behold, look upon, gaze at, contemplate, and examine those who cause strife, those who cause quarrels, those who are hostile,
those who are antagonistic, those who have been struck down, those who have struck back, those who have been injured,
and those who have injured others.”
"Behold people as a disease!
I shall proclaim agitation. Agitation means:
perturbation, trepidation, terror, fear, oppression, disturbance, calamity, and misfortune.
"I shall praise" means: I shall extol, declare, teach, prescribe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and explain.
Thus, "I shall praise [the sense of] urgency" means: I shall praise it as it has been realized by me.
"Just as I have stirred myself, agitated myself, and brought about a sense of spiritual urgency within myself"—
this is how I was stirred.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Fear has arisen from those who wield the rod against themselves;
behold the people in their turmoil!
I shall proclaim the sense of spiritual urgency.”
"Just as it has been understood by me. Having seen the world quivering like fish in shallow water, [he said: "Just as it has been understood by me."
Seeing them hostile toward one another, fear entered me.
"Seeing the generation trembling" means: [seeing them] in a state of agitation.
“Pajā” is a designation for beings.
Beings are quivering with the quivering of craving, quivering with the quivering of views,
and quivering with the quivering of defilements.
trembling with the trembling of misconduct,
trembling with the trembling of effort,
and trembling with the trembling of karmic result.
One who is stained, quivering with lust;
one who is corrupted, quivering with hatred;
one who is deluded, quivering with ignorance.
Bound by conceit and flickering,
seized by views and flickering,
fallen into distraction and flickering.
One who has gone to what is undesirable, quivering with doubt;
one who has become firm-rooted, quivering with underlying tendencies;
and one who quivers because of gain.
Trembling because of non-gain,
trembling because of fame,
trembling because of ill-repute,
Trembling at praise,
trembling at blame,
trembling at pleasure,
Trembling because of suffering,
trembling because of birth,
trembling because of old age.
trembling with disease,
trembling with death,
and trembling with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
Trembling with the suffering of the hell realms,
trembling with the suffering of the animal womb,
and trembling with the suffering of the realm of hungry ghosts.
Trembling with human suffering, with suffering rooted in the descent into the womb,
and with suffering rooted in the stay in the womb...
the suffering rooted in emerging from the womb;
the suffering connected to being born; and the suffering pertaining to what is acquired after being born.
by suffering through one's own exertion … by suffering through the exertion of others … by the suffering of suffering …
by the suffering of conditioned formations … by the suffering of change … by the suffering of eye-disease …
... by disease of the ear ...
by disease of the nose ...
by disease of the tongue ...
... by a disease of the body ... by a disease of the head ...
by a disease of the ear ...
...by disease of the mouth ...
by disease of the teeth ...
by cough ...
... by rheumatism ... by catarrh ...
by burning fever ...
... by old age ...
by a stomach ailment ...
by fainting ...
...of dysentery ...
of piercing pain ...
of cholera ...
... with leprosy ...
with boils ...
with ringworm ...
By cold...
by hunger...
by burning heat...
...itching ...
scabies ...
ringworm ...
... with a file ...
with blood ...
with bile ...
... by diabetes mellitus ... by a shoulder [injury] ...
by an abscess ...
... for hemorrhoids ...
for a disease arising from bile ...
for a disease arising from phlegm ...
by a disease arising from wind … by a disease arising from a combination of humors … by a disease arising from a change in the seasons …
by an affliction arising from the avoidance of unevenness...
by an affliction resulting from external trauma...
by an affliction born of the ripening of kamma...
by cold … by heat … by hunger …
... for thirst ...
for urination ... for defecation ...
... by the suffering of contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles;
... by the suffering of the mother’s death; ...
by the suffering of the father’s death; ...
by the suffering of a brother’s death … by the suffering of a sister’s death … by the suffering of a son’s death …
by the suffering of a daughter’s death … by the suffering of a relative’s death … by the suffering of the loss of wealth …

Trembling, quivering, fluttering, shaking, trembling violently, and shaking all over because of the suffering of illness, the suffering of the loss of virtue, and the suffering of the loss of right view.
"Having seen": having seen, having beheld, having weighed, having scrutinized, having discerned, having made manifest—having seen the generation trembling.
"As fish in scant water": as fish when there is little water, when water is exhausted, [are pursued] by crows or hawks...
Just as fish in shallow water, being pursued by crows or cranes, are tossed about, seized, and devoured, quivering, trembling, shaking, writhing, and convulsing;
even so, this generation quivers through the quivering of craving... [and so on].
"They quiver, quiver intensely, and quiver violently; they tremble, tremble intensely, and tremble violently because of the suffering of the calamity of wrong views—just like fish in shallow water.
"Hostile toward one another" means that beings are hostile, opposed, struck, counter-struck, provoked, and counter-provoked by one another.
Kings dispute with kings, kshatriyas dispute with kshatriyas, brahmins dispute with brahmins,
householders dispute with householders; even a mother disputes with her son, a son disputes with his mother, a father disputes with his son,
a son disputes with his father, and a brother disputes with a brother.
A sister quarrels with her sister, a brother quarrels with his sister, a sister quarrels with her brother,
and a companion quarrels with his companion;
having fallen into strife, contention, and dispute there, they attack one another with their hands and attack one another with clods of earth.
They attack with sticks, they attack with weapons; there they meet death or suffering equal to death—being mutually hostile.
Seeing this, fear entered me.

"Having seen" means having seen, having looked at, having weighed, having scrutinized, having discerned, having made manifest: "Fear, affliction, collision, calamity, misfortune, and invasion have entered me"—thus, "having seen, fear has entered me.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Seeing the world struggling,
like fish in shallow water,
hostile toward one another, [I have gone forth].”
"Seeing this, fear has entered me:
the world is entirely without essence,
and all directions are trembling."
Desiring my own dwelling,
I did not see it as unestablished;
[I saw that] the world is entirely without essence.

“World” means the world of hell, the world of animals, the world of hungry ghosts, the world of humans, the world of devas; the world of aggregates, the world of elements, the world of sense bases; this world and the other world; the Brahma-world and the deva-world—this is called “the world.

The world of hell is without essence, devoid of essence, stripped of essence—whether by way of the essence of permanence, the essence of happiness, or the essence of self; it is not permanent, not stable, not eternal, and not subject to changelessness.
The world of the animal realm… the world of the sphere of hungry ghosts… the world of human beings…
the world of the gods … the world of the aggregates … the world of the elements …
The world of the sense bases… this world… the other world…
The world of Brahmā...

the world of the devas is pithless, sapless, devoid of essence—whether by way of the essence of permanence, the essence of happiness, or the essence of a self; or by way of what is permanent, stable, eternal, or subject to no change.
Just as a reed is pithless, sapless, and devoid of essence, so too is a castor-oil plant pithless, sapless, and devoid of essence.
Just as the udumbara tree is without core, sapless, and devoid of essence; just as the setakaccha tree is without core, sapless, and devoid of essence;
just as the pāribhaddaka tree is without core, sapless, and devoid of essence; just as a mass of foam is without core, sapless, and devoid of essence;
just as a bubble on the water is without core, sapless, and devoid of essence; just as a mirage is without core, sapless, and devoid of essence.
Just as the trunk of a plantain tree is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core;

just as an illusion is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core—even so the world of hell is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core, whether by way of a core of permanence, a core of happiness, or a core of self; or by way of being permanent, stable, eternal, or subject to non-change.
So too is the world of animal birth...
The world of hungry ghosts, the world of humans,

and the world of devas are without essence, devoid of essence, and lacking in essence— whether by way of the essence of permanence, the essence of happiness, or the essence of a self; they are not permanent, not stable, not eternal, and not subject to the nature of non-change.
The world of aggregates … the world of elements … the world of sense bases …
This world … the other world … the Brahma-world …

"The world of the gods is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core; it is not possessed of the core of permanence, nor the core of happiness, nor the core of self; it is not permanent, stable, eternal, or subject to non-change"—thus the world is entirely without core.
"All directions are shaken."
Whatever formations there are in the eastern direction— whether stirred, moved, shaken, or struck— they are followed by birth through impermanence,
pursued by aging, overcome by sickness, assailed by death, established in suffering,
and are without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and have become a state of no-refuge.
Whatever formations are in the western direction… whatever formations are in the northern direction… whatever formations are in the southern direction…

Whatever formations there are in the eastern intermediate direction … whatever formations there are in the western intermediate direction … whatever formations there are in the northern intermediate direction …
Whatever formations are in the southern intermediate direction...
whatever formations are in the lower direction...
whatever formations are in the upper direction...
Whatever conditioned phenomena exist in the ten directions, they too are stirred, shaken, moved, and struck; they are followed by birth through impermanence,
pursued by aging, overcome by sickness, assailed by death, established in suffering,
and without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and having become a state of no-refuge.
And this has also been said:
“Even though that celestial mansion of yours is ablaze,
illuminating the northern quarter;”
Seeing conflict in form and its constant trembling,
the wise person does not delight in form;
the world is struck down by death.
Enveloped by old age,
pierced by the dart of craving,
he is constantly smoldering with desire.
The entire world is set ablaze;
the entire world is smoking;
the entire world is burning.
“The entire world has trembled;
all directions have quaked.
I wish for nothing more than my own dwelling.”
"Desiring one's own dwelling"— meaning desiring, accepting, longing for, yearning for, and craving it as a refuge, a shelter, a retreat, a resort,
and a final goal. "I did not see you dwelling there."
I saw only that which is clung to; I saw nothing unclung to. All youth has been overtaken by old age;
all health has been overtaken by illness; all life has been overtaken by death; all gain has been overtaken by loss;
all fame has been overtaken by disrepute; all praise has been overtaken by blame; all pleasure has been overtaken by pain.
“Gain and loss, fame and disrepute,
blame and praise, pleasure and pain—
these conditions among human beings are impermanent.”
“Impermanent, subject to change”—
I did not see anything that was not so.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The world is entirely without essence;
all directions are shaken.
Desiring my own dwelling,”
"I did not see him, nor was he fed.
But when he had been dismissed and remained hostile,
a sense of dissatisfaction arose within me upon seeing this.
Then here I beheld the dart,
difficult to see, lodged within the heart;
it was at the very end that I became free from enmity.
"But at the end" means: old age brings all youth to an end; illness brings all health to an end;
death brings all life to an end; non-gain brings all gain to an end; disrepute brings all fame to an end;
blame brings all praise to an end; and suffering brings all happiness to an end.
But at the end, indeed. "Hostile" means: beings who desire youth are hostile toward old age; beings who desire health are hostile toward illness;
beings who desire life are hostile toward death; beings who desire gain are hostile toward loss; beings who desire fame...
Beings are opposed to dishonor; beings who desire praise are opposed to blame;
beings who desire happiness are opposed to suffering. When they are struck, struck back, provoked, and provoked back, they are indeed hostile at the end.
"Upon seeing it, aversion arose in me.
"Seeing" means having seen, having looked upon, having weighed, having judged, having discerned, having made manifest— thus, "seeing."
‘I have aversion’ means: whatever aversion, whatever lack of delight, whatever lack of enjoyment, whatever longing, whatever distress there was—having seen this, “I had aversion” arose.
Then, “I saw the dart herein.”
Now, "atha" is a phonetic junction (*padasandhi*) ... [and so on] ... this is the sequential order of words (*padānupubbatā*):
namely, "atha.
"Ettha" means "among beings."
"Arrows" refers to seven arrows:
the arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, the arrow of delusion, the arrow of conceit, the arrow of views, the arrow of sorrow, and the arrow of doubt.
"He saw" means he saw, he perceived, he beheld, and he penetrated.
Then, right here, I saw the dart,
seated within the heart, so difficult to see.
"Difficult to see" means it is hard to see, hard to perceive, hard to behold, hard to understand, hard to comprehend, and hard to penetrate.
Difficult to see.
"Dependent on the heart" (*hadayassita*): by "heart" (*hadaya*) is meant consciousness (*citta*).

That which is consciousness, mind (*mano*), mentality (*mānasa*), heart, the pure (*paṇḍara*), the mind-base (*manāyatana*), the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding element of mind-consciousness.

“Dependent on the heart” means dependent on the heart, dependent on consciousness, dependent on mind, accompanied by mind, co-nascent, conjoined, associated, arising together, ceasing together, having a single basis, and having a single object— thus,
that which is dependent on the heart is difficult to see.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“When the dispute was ended,
seeing that, aversion arose in me;
then I beheld the arrow here.”
Difficult to see, yet cherished in the heart.
Pierced by which dart, one runs hither and thither in all directions.
Having extracted that very dart,
one neither runs about nor sinks down.
One who is pierced by that dart runs hither and thither in all directions.
"Arrows": there are seven arrows—
the arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, the arrow of delusion, the arrow of conceit, the arrow of views, the arrow of sorrow, and the arrow of doubt.
What is the arrow of lust?
That which is lust, infatuation, inclination, compliance, the lust of delight, infatuation of the mind... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness—this is the arrow of lust.
What is the dart of hatred?
“He has done me harm,” thus resentment arises; “He is doing me harm,” thus resentment arises; “He will do me harm,” thus resentment arises...
[and so on] ...fury, abruptness, and displeasure of mind.
This is the dart of hatred.
What is the dart of delusion? Ignorance regarding suffering … [and so on] … [up to] … ignorance regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is the dart of delusion.
Ignorance regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering; ignorance regarding the past; ignorance regarding the future; ignorance regarding both the past and the future;

ignorance regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena. Whatever is such non-seeing, non-comprehension, non-awakening, non-enlightenment, non-penetration, non-grasping, non-exploration, non-contemplation, non-reviewing, lack of direct realization, dullness, folly, delusion, extreme delusion, and total bewilderment—[this is ignorance].

Ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the snare of ignorance, delusion, and the unwholesome root— this is the dart of delusion.
What is the dart of conceit?
The conceit, “I am superior”; the conceit, “I am equal”; the conceit, “I am inferior.

Whatever such conceit there is—this imagining, this state of imagining, this loftiness, this exaltation, this banner, this grasping, this desire for self-display of the mind—this is the dart of conceit.
What is the barb of views?
It is the embodiment-view with twenty bases, the false view with ten bases, and the extreme view with ten bases.
Such a view as this is a resort to views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, and a vacillation of views.
The fetter of views, grasping, seizing, adherence, misapprehension, the wrong path, the false course, falsehood,

the sphere of sectarianism, the grasping of inversion, the grasping of the perverted, the grasping of distortion, the wrong grasp, the grasping of what is not as it truly is as being "as it truly is"—
namely, the sixty-two types of speculative views.
This is the dart of views.
What is the dart of sorrow?
It is [the sorrow] of one who has been struck by misfortune concerning relatives, or struck by misfortune concerning illness, or struck by misfortune concerning wealth.

For one who is touched by the ruin of virtue, or touched by the ruin of view, or possessed of this or that misfortune, or touched by this or that state of suffering—there is sorrow, grieving, the state of being grieved;
inward sorrow, inward anguish, inward burning, inward fever; the consuming of the mind, and dejection.
This is the dart of sorrow.

What is the dart of doubt? It is doubt regarding suffering, doubt regarding the origin of suffering, doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, and doubt regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

Doubt regarding the practice, doubt regarding the past, doubt regarding the future, doubt regarding both the past and the future, and doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality (idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppanna).

Whatever is of such a nature as doubt, doubting, the state of having doubted, perplexity, uncertainty, vacillation, the path of duality, hesitation, grasping at various sides, shrinking back, running about, lack of penetration, paralysis of the mind, mental distress—
this is the arrow of "how-is-it-ness" (kathaṅkathāsalla).
"Pierced by which dart one runs in all directions":
pierced, struck, touched, overcome, obsessed, and possessed by the dart of lust, one engages in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind;
one kills living beings and takes what is not given.
He breaks into houses, carries off plunder, commits burglary, lies in ambush, commits adultery, and speaks falsehoods.
Thus, pierced, struck, afflicted, overcome, deluded, and possessed by the arrow of passion, he runs, runs about, runs hither and thither, and wanders through the cycle of existence.
Or else, pierced, struck, afflicted, overcome, infatuated, and possessed by the dart of passion, he plunges into the great ocean by ship while seeking wealth.
Forewarned by cold, forewarned by heat, oppressed by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and perishing from hunger and thirst,
he goes to Tiṅguṇa, he goes to Takola, he goes to Takkasilā.
He goes to Kāḷamukha; he goes to Purapūra; he goes to Vesuṅga;
he goes to Verāpatha; he goes to Java; he goes to Tāmali; he goes to Vaṅka; he goes to Eḷabandhana;
he goes to Suvaṇṇakūṭa; he goes to Suvaṇṇabhūmi; he goes to Tambapaṇṇi; he goes to Suppāraka; he goes to Bhārukaccha.
He goes to Suraṭṭha; he goes to Bhaṅgaloka; he goes to Bhaṅgaṇa; he goes to Paramabhaṅgaṇa;
he goes to Yona; he goes to Paramayona; he goes to Vinaka; he goes to Mūlapada;
he goes to the Maru wilderness; he goes by the path for knees; he goes by the path for goats; he goes by the path for rams.

He goes along a path of thorns, he goes along a path of sunshades, he goes along a path of bamboo, he goes along a path of birds, he goes along a path of mice, he goes along a path of demons, he goes along a path of creepers;
while searching, he does not find it, and he experiences pain and grief rooted in non-acquisition. While searching...
Having acquired them, he experiences suffering and mental distress rooted in guarding, thinking:
"How can it be that kings do not seize my wealth, nor thieves steal it, nor fire burn it, nor water carry it away, nor unloved heirs take it?
While he is thus guarding and protecting it, those possessions are destroyed; he experiences suffering and mental distress rooted in separation.
In this way, pierced, struck, touched, overcome, deluded, and possessed by the dart of lust, one runs, runs about, hastens, and wanders through the cycle of existence.
[Likewise] by the dart of hatred...
by the dart of delusion...
Overcome by the dart of the mind, pierced, struck, afflicted, obsessed, and possessed, one engages in misconduct of body,
misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; one kills living beings, takes what is not given,
breaks into dwellings, commits robbery, acts as a housebreaker, and stands as a highwayman.
He goes to another’s wife and speaks falsehoods.
Thus, pierced, struck, touched, overcome, deluded, and possessed by the dart of the mind, he runs, runs about, runs hither and thither, and wanders through the cycle of existence.

Pierced, struck, touched, overcome, deluded, and possessed by the dart of views, he becomes a naked ascetic, one who lives without restraint, one who scrapes his hands clean, one who does not accept the invitation "Come, venerable sir," nor the invitation "Stay, venerable sir";
He does not accept what has been brought from a shop, nor what is prepared specifically for him, nor does he consent to an invitation;
he does not receive food from the mouth of a storage jar, nor from the mouth of a basket, nor across a sheepskin, nor across a staff, nor across a pestle;
he does not receive food from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing, nor from a woman in the presence of her husband.
He eats at alms-gatherings, but not where the food is set out, nor where flies are swarming.
He does not eat fish or meat; he does not drink fermented liquor, spirits, or grain-beer.
He is a "one-house" eater or a "one-bite" eater, or he is a "two-house" eater or a "two-bite" eater... [and so on].
He is one who eats at a single house or one who eats at seven houses.
He subsists on a single gift, or he subsists on two gifts …pe… or he subsists on as many as seven gifts.
He takes food once a day, or he takes food once every two days...
[and so on] ...or he takes food once every seven days.
Thus, in such a manner, he dwells devoted to the practice of taking meals at intervals, even for half a month.
Thus, pierced, struck, touched, overcome, deluded, and possessed by the dart of views, one runs, runs about, runs hither and thither,

and wanders through the cycle of existence. Or else, pierced, struck, touched, overcome, deluded, and possessed by the dart of views, one becomes a consumer of greens, or a consumer of millet, or a consumer of wild rice, or a consumer of coarse grain, or a consumer of gleanings.
Or he eats only one meal a day; or he eats at every fourth mealtime; or he subsists on a single handful of food; or he eats only once a month;

or he lives by eating only once a fortnight. He eats grass, or eats cow dung, or eats rice-scum, or eats oil-cake, or eats sesame seeds, or eats grass, or eats cow dung, or subsists on forest roots and fruits, living on whatever fruit has fallen.
He wears hemp garments, or garments of hemp-mixed cloth, or shrouds from a cemetery, or rag-robes from a dust heap.
He wears garments made of bark-fiber; he wears deerskins; he wears a cloak of antelope hide; he wears a garment of kusa grass; he wears a garment of bark;
he wears a garment of wood-shavings; he wears a blanket of human hair; he wears a wing-robe of owls’ feathers;
he becomes one who plucks out his hair and beard, dwelling devoted to the practice of plucking out his hair and beard.
He is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats; he is one who squats, devoted to the practice of squatting;
he uses a bed of thorns, he makes his bed on a bed of thorns; he makes his bed on a plank, he makes his bed on the bare ground;
he uses a single garment, wearing dust and dirt; he is one who lives in the open air, sleeping wherever he happens to be; he is one who eats only what is left over.

He is devoted to the practice of eating disgusting food; he is one who abstains from drink, devoted to the practice of not drinking; and he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water three times a day, including the evening.
Thus, in such ways, he dwells devoted to various kinds of practices for the mortification and tormenting of the body.
In this way, one who is immersed, pierced, struck, overcome, deluded, and possessed by the dart of views runs, rushes about, wanders, and transmigrates.
One who is immersed, pierced, struck, overcome, deluded, and possessed by the dart of sorrow grieves, languishes, laments, beats one's breast, weeps, and falls into confusion.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Once upon a time, brahmin, the mother of a certain woman in this very Sāvatthī passed away.
Because of her death, she became insane and deranged; wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, she would say:
‘Have you seen my mother? Have you seen my mother?’”
In the past, brahmin, in this very Sāvatthī, the father of a certain woman died...
the brother died...
the sister died...
A son died; a daughter died;
a husband died.
Upon his death, she became insane and deranged; wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, she would say:
“Have you seen my husband? Have you seen my husband?
Once in the past, brahmin, the mother of a certain man in this very Sāvatthī passed away.
Because of her death, he became insane and deranged; wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, he would say:
“Have you seen my mother? Have you seen my mother?
Once in the past, brahmin, the father of a certain man in this very Sāvatthī passed away…
A brother has passed away… a sister has passed away… a son has passed away…
His daughter died… his wife died.
Because of her death, he became insane and deranged; wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, he spoke thus:
“Have you seen my wife? Have you seen my wife?
“Once upon a time, brahmin, a certain woman from this very Sāvatthī went to her relatives’ home.
Her relatives wished to take away her husband and give him to another, but she did not want that.”
Then that woman said this to her husband:
“Noble son, these relatives of mine wish to take you away from me and give you to another; let us both die.
Then that man, having cut the woman in two, threw himself into a pit.
‘We shall both exist after death.
Thus, pierced, struck, touched, overcome, bewildered, and possessed by the dart of sorrow, one runs, runs about, runs hither and thither, and wanders through saṃsāra.
Pierced, struck, touched, overcome, bewildered, and possessed by the dart of doubt, one becomes fallen into uncertainty, fallen into perplexity, and born of indecision.
“Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past?
Having been what, what did I become in the past? Shall I exist in the future? Shall I not exist in the future?”
"What indeed shall I become in the future? How indeed shall I become in the future?
Having been what, what indeed shall I become in the future? Or, regarding the present time, one is inwardly full of doubt:
"Do I exist? Do I not exist? What indeed am I? How indeed [am I]?"
"I am [such-and-such]; from where has this being come, and where will it go?
Thus, pierced, struck, overwhelmed, confounded, and possessed by the arrow of doubt, one runs, rushes about, wanders, and transmigrates.
One conditions those very arrows.

Constructing those arrows, by way of the construction of arrows, he runs toward the eastern direction, he runs toward the western direction, he runs toward the northern direction, he runs toward the southern direction.
Those constructions of arrows are not abandoned;
because those constructions of arrows are not abandoned, he runs toward a state of existence, he runs toward hell, [he runs] toward the animal womb.
It runs; it runs in the realm of ghosts, it runs in the world of humans, it runs in the world of devas;

from destiny to destiny, from rebirth to rebirth, from rebirth-linking to rebirth-linking, from existence to existence, from saṃsāra to saṃsāra, from the cycle to the cycle—it runs, runs about, runs along, and wanders through the round.
"Pierced by which dart one runs hither and thither in all directions;
having extracted that very dart, one neither runs nor sinks.
This refers to the dart of lust, the dart of hatred, the dart of delusion, the dart of conceit, the dart of views, the dart of sorrow, and the dart of doubt.
Having pulled out, having pulled out thoroughly; having extracted, having extracted thoroughly; having torn up, having torn up thoroughly;

having abandoned, having dispelled, having brought to an end, having caused to cease—neither does it run toward the eastern direction, nor does it run toward the western direction, nor does it run toward the northern direction, nor does it run toward the southern direction.
Those formations associated with the dart have been abandoned;
because formations associated with the dart have been abandoned, one does not run toward rebirth, does not run toward hell, does not run toward the animal realm,
does not run toward the sphere of hungry ghosts, does not run toward the world of humans, and does not run toward the world of devas.

One does not run, rush, hasten, or wander through the cycle of rebirth by means of a destiny, nor by means of a birth, nor by means of a rebirth-linking, nor by means of an existence, nor by means of saṃsāra, nor by means of the round.
Having extracted that very dart, one no longer runs.

"He does not sink" means he does not sink in the flood of sensual desire, he does not sink in the flood of existence, he does not sink in the flood of views, he does not sink in the flood of ignorance;
he does not settle, he does not submerge, he does not despair, he does not go away, he does not depart—having extracted that very dart, he neither runs nor sinks.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Pierced by that arrow,
one runs in all directions;
having pulled out that very arrow, [one should remain still].”
"It does not run, nor does it sink.
In that regard, those things which are clung to in the world are praised as training.
One should not be intent upon those things;
having become completely disillusioned with all sensual pleasures,
one should train for one’s own Nibbāna.
In this context, "the trainings are sung" refers to those things which are celebrated in the world.

"Trainings" (*sikkhā*) means: training in elephants, training in horses, training in chariots, training in archery, surgery (*sālākiya*), medicine for arrow wounds (*sallakattiya*), the science of bodily treatments (*kāyatikiccha*), the science of prosperity (*bhūtiya*), and pediatrics (*komārabhacca*).
"Are sung" (*anugīyanti*) means they are sung, chanted, spoken, recited, explained, and expressed in common usage.
Alternatively, they are sung, grasped, learned, retained, mastered, and characterized for the sake of obtaining what is cherished.
What is called "cherished" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure:
forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; [and likewise sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects].
Sounds cognizable by the ear ... [and so on] ...
odors cognizable by the nose ...
tastes cognizable by the tongue ...

Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—for what reason are the five strands of sensual pleasure called "addictions"?

Because for the most part gods and humans desire, relish, long for, crave, and yearn for the five strands of sensual pleasure; for that reason, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called "addictions."
"In the world" means "in the world of human beings"—
therein the trainings are sung forth, those things which are clung to in the world.
One should not be intent upon them.

One should not be intent upon those trainings or those five strands of sensual pleasure; one should not be inclined toward them, not prone to them, not leaning toward them, not devoted to them, and not dominated by them—one should not be intent upon them.
Having become completely disillusioned with them, one abandons all sensual desires.
“Nibbijjhati” means having penetrated [the truth].
Having penetrated that “all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” and having penetrated that “all conditioned phenomena are suffering,” and so forth...
Having penetrated the truth that “whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation,” [he understands] “all. “All” means:
this is a term for consuming everything—every single thing, in every way, entirely, without remainder, and without exception.
This is what is meant by “all.”
Regarding "sensual pleasures" (kāmā): in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasure—sensual pleasure as objects (vatthukāmā) and sensual pleasure as defilements (kilesakāmā).
… [as follows] … these are called sensual pleasure as objects. … [as follows] …
These are called the defilements of sensual desire;
having become utterly disillusioned with all sensual desires,
one should train for the sake of Nibbāna alone.
Training means the three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom …pe… this is the training in higher wisdom.
Thinking, "I am one for whom only Nibbāna remains," for the sake of extinguishing one's own lust, for the sake of extinguishing hatred, for the sake of extinguishing delusion—
and so on— for the sake of the calming, the pacifying, the subsiding, the extinguishing, the relinquishing,
and the tranquilization of all unwholesome volitional formations, one should train in the higher virtue, one should train in the higher mind, and one should train in the higher wisdom.
Reflecting upon these three trainings, one should train; knowing them, one should train...
[and so on] ...realizing that which is to be realized, one should train, practice, practice thoroughly, and live having undertaken them—thus one trains for one’s own Nibbāna.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“In that regard, those things which are clung to in the world are sung as trainings.”
One should not be intent upon them,
but having become utterly disillusioned with all sensual pleasures,
one should train for one’s own Nibbāna.
One may indeed be free from immodesty,
devoid of deceit and empty slander,
and free from anger and the evil of greed.
The sage should cross over doubt.
"He should be truthful and free from arrogance":
"He should be truthful" means he should be endowed with truthful speech, he should be endowed with right view, and he should be endowed with the noble eightfold path.
One should be honest.
"Modest" refers to the three types of immodesty:
bodily immodesty, verbal immodesty, and mental immodesty …pe…
This is the mental state of insolence (*pāgabbhiya*).

One for whom these three forms of insolence have been abandoned, eradicated, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge—such a person is called "free from insolence" (*appagabbha*);
thus one may truly be free from insolence.
"Devoid of deceit and empty of slander.
Deceit is said to be a deceptive conduct.
Here, someone, having practiced misconduct with the body, having practiced misconduct with speech, and having practiced misconduct with the mind—
For the sake of concealing that, he forms an evil desire: he wishes, "May they not know me";
he intends, "May they not know me"; he utters the words, "May they not know me"; he exerts himself with the body, "May they not know me.

Such as this is deceit, being deceitful, transgression, deception, guile, dissimulation, evasion, hiding, concealing, covering up, shielding, the act of not revealing, the act of not making manifest, the act of concealing, the performance of evil deeds.
This is called deceit (*māyā*).

One for whom this deceit has been abandoned, eradicated, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—such a person is called one free from deceit (*amāyo*).
"Empty of backbiting" (*rittapesuṇo*): here, "backbiting" refers to a certain person who is a backbiter... [and so on].
Thus one instigates malicious talebearing with the intention of causing division.

One for whom this malicious talebearing has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, for whom it is incapable of arising again and has been burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called one who is empty of malicious talebearing, secluded from malicious talebearing, and utterly secluded from malicious talebearing:
he is "free from guile and empty of malicious talebearing."
"The sage, free from anger, should cross over the evil of greed and doubt.
Now, although it is said "free from anger," anger itself must first be discussed.
Anger arises in ten ways.
“‘He has done me harm’—thus anger arises...
[as before] ... One for whom this anger has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge, is called one who is without anger.
He is without anger because anger has been abandoned; he is without anger because the basis for anger has been fully understood; he is without anger because the cause of anger has been severed.”
Greed is that which is greed, the state of being greedy, the state of being obsessed...
covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
Avarice is said to be the five kinds of stinginess.
Stinginess regarding dwellings...
[and so forth] ...grasping is called stinginess. "The Sage" (muni): [this refers to one who has abandoned such grasping].
"Mona" is said to be knowledge... [as before] ...having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage (*muni*).
"The sage, free from anger, crosses over the evil of greed and doubt"—thus the sage has crossed over, traversed, leaped across, surmounted, and gone beyond both the evil of greed and doubt.
Free from anger, the sage should cross over the evil of greed and doubt.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"One should be truthful and free from arrogance..."
Free from deceit, empty of slander,
without anger, and having overcome the evil of greed and stinginess—
the sage transcends all.
One should endure sleepiness, sloth, and lethargy;
one should not dwell in negligence;
one should not abide in arrogance.
"A person whose mind is set on Nibbāna endures sleepiness, lethargy, and sloth. Regarding "sleepiness" (*niddā*):

it is the body’s lack of well-being, lack of serviceability, constriction, envelopment, internal obstruction, drowsiness, nodding, blinking, sleeping, the act of sleeping, and the state of being asleep.

"Lassitude" (*tandi*) means lassitude, the state of being languid, the condition of having become languid, the act of becoming languid; it is idleness, the state of idleness, the condition of having become idle.

"Sloth" (*thīna*) means the mind's lack of health, its unwieldiness, its sinking, its deep sinking, its sluggishness, the state of sluggishness, its sinking, the act of sinking, the condition of having become sluggish; it is dullness, the state of dullness, the condition of having become dull of mind.
"Sloth and lassitude together" refers to sloth and lassitude combined.
“He would endure, withstand, overcome, surmount, exhaust, and subdue drowsiness, lethargy, and sloth”—
thus he endures drowsiness, lethargy, and sloth;
he does not dwell in negligence.
Heedlessness should be described in terms of misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, or misconduct of mind; or in terms of the five cords of sensual pleasure.

It is the slackening of the mind, the failure to produce such slackening, or the lack of earnestness in practice, the lack of constancy in practice, the lack of steadfastness in practice, a state of sluggishness, the laying aside of desire, and the laying aside of the burden with regard to the cultivation of wholesome states.
Non-cultivation, non-development, non-repetition, lack of resolve, lack of application, and negligence.
Whatever is such negligence, the act of being negligent, and the state of being negligent—
this is called negligence (*pamāda*).
"One should not dwell with negligence; one should not dwell with negligence, should not live with it, should not abide with it, should not remain with it.
One should abandon negligence, dispel it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease.

One should be detached from negligence, abstain from it, refrain from it, have emerged from it, be escaped from it, and be liberated from it. One should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries."
"One should not dwell in negligence;
one should not stand in conceit.
Herein, "conceit" means that someone here despises another on account of birth, or clan, or for some other reason whatsoever.
Whatever kind of conceit there is— conceiving, the state of having conceived, loftiness, haughtiness, a banner, grasping, or the desire for a standard in the mind—
this is called overweening conceit (*atimāna*).
"One should not stand in overweening conceit" means this.
One should not stand in conceit, one should not persist in conceit; one should abandon conceit, dispel it, bring it to an end, cause it to cease, and lead it to non-existence.
One should be detached from conceit, abstain from it, refrain from it, have emerged from it, have escaped it, and be fully liberated from it;
one should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries—thus it is said.
"One should not stand in conceit;
a person whose mind is set on Nibbāna.
Here, a certain person, while giving gifts, undertaking moral discipline, performing the Uposatha rites, [providing] drinking water and water for washing—
While attending to his duties, sweeping the courtyard, worshipping the shrine, offering perfumes and garlands at the shrine, circumambulating the shrine,
and performing whatever wholesome volitional formations belonging to the three realms, he does so not for the sake of a destination, not for the sake of rebirth, not for the sake of re-linking,
not for the sake of existence, not for the sake of saṃsāra, and not for the sake of the round; all of it—
With the intention of disjunction, he forms [volitional formations] that incline toward Nibbāna, lean toward Nibbāna, and tend toward Nibbāna;
thus too is a person whose mind is set on Nibbāna.
Or alternatively, having turned the mind away from the element of all conditioned formations, he directs the mind toward the deathless element.
“This is peaceful, this is sublime: namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Thus a person whose mind is set on Nibbāna [thinks]:
“The wise do not, for the sake of the pleasure of acquisitions, [strive for it].”
They give gifts for the sake of renewed existence;
yet they also give gifts for the sake of the complete destruction of the acquisitions, so that there is no further becoming.
The wise do not cultivate meditative absorptions for the sake of the pleasure of acquisitions or for the sake of renewed existence; rather,
they do so indeed for the complete destruction of acquisitions.
They develop jhāna for the sake of non-renewal of existence.
With hearts inclined toward that and resolved upon that,
they give gifts while aspiring for Nibbāna.
"Just as rivers that have entered the midst of the ocean become destined for extinction (nibbāna),
so too does the person whose mind is set on nibbāna."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Endure drowsiness and sloth;
do not dwell in negligence.”
A person whose mind is set on Nibbāna should not stand in pride,
nor should they yield to the deception of falsehood.
One should not form attachment to form;
one should thoroughly understand conceit and live free from rashness.
"One should not be led away by a lie.
A lie is called false speech.
Here, someone, having been summoned as a witness and questioned in an assembly, in a gathering, in the midst of kinsmen, in the midst of a guild, or in the presence of the royal court, [says:]
"Come now, good man, say what you know," he said;
and he, not knowing, said, "I know," or knowing, said, "I do not know."
Either not seeing, he says, “I see,” or seeing, he says,
“I do not see. Thus, for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of some trifling material gain, he speaks a deliberate falsehood.
This is called false speech.
Furthermore, [it is established] by three modes...
or by four modes...
In five ways … in six ways … in seven ways …
In eight ways ... [as above] ...
through these eight ways there is false speech.
One should not be led away by deceptive speech.
One should not go on a journey involving false speech, nor depart on one, nor drive one, nor collect for one; one should abandon false speech, dispel it, bring it to an end, cause its non-existence;
one should be aloof from false speech, abstain from it, refrain from it, have departed from it, emerged from it, and be liberated from it;
one should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries and is detached from it.
One should not be led astray by conceit.
One should not form attachment to form.
"Form" refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
"One should not form affection for form" means:

one should not make affection for form, one should not make desire, one should not make love, one should not make lust; one should not produce it, one should not generate it, one should not bring it about, one should not cause it to arise—that is, "one should not form affection for form."
"And one should fully understand conceit.
Conceit: by way of a single classification, conceit is the inflation of the mind.
Pride is twofold:
pride in self-exaltation and pride in disparaging others.
Pride is threefold:
the pride of thinking "I am superior," the pride of thinking "I am equal," and [the pride of thinking "I am inferior"].
The conceit, “I am inferior.
There are four ways in which conceit arises:
one generates conceit because of gain.
Through gain one generates conceit;
through praise one generates conceit;
through pleasure one generates conceit.
Pride is fivefold:
one generates pride thinking, "I am a recipient of pleasing forms," and "I am a recipient of pleasing sounds" ... [and so on].
...of odors ...
of tastes ...
of tangibles," he generates conceit.
Pride in six ways:
one generates pride through the possession of the eye; through the possession of the ear... [and so on].
... for the excellence of the nose ...
for the excellence of the tongue ...
for the excellence of the body ...
Through the perfection of the mind, one generates conceit.
There are seven kinds of conceit: overweening conceit (*atimāna*), [inferiority conceit, equality conceit, conceit, great conceit, conceit of "I am," and the conceit "I am better"].
Conceit, overweening conceit,
self-depreciation, and conceit of equality.
excessive pride,
the pride of "I am," and false pride.
Pride is eightfold:
through gain one generates pride;
through loss one generates self-depreciation.
Through fame one generates conceit;
through disrepute one generates self-depreciation;
through praise one generates conceit.
Through blame, one generates self-depreciation;
through pleasure, one generates pride;
through pain, one generates self-depreciation.
Pride is of nine kinds:
the pride of one who is superior thinking,
"I am superior," and the pride of one who is superior thinking, "I am equal."
The conceit "I am inferior" in one who is superior;
the conceit "I am superior" in one who is equal;
the conceit "I am equal" in one who is equal.
The conceit "I am inferior" in one who is equal;
the conceit "I am superior" in one who is inferior;
and the conceit "I am equal" in one who is inferior.
The conceit of one who is inferior, thinking, “I am inferior.
Conceit is tenfold:
here someone generates conceit on account of birth, or clan, or [any other basis] up to any particular ground whatsoever.
Whatever such conceit, the act of conceiving, the state of having conceived, loftiness, haughtiness, flagging, grasping, the desire for a banner of the mind—
this is called conceit.
"And one should fully understand conceit" means this.
One should fully understand conceit through three kinds of full understanding:
through the full understanding of the known, through the full understanding by scrutinization, and through the full understanding by abandoning.
...by means of the full understanding of abandoning. What is the full understanding of knowing?
One knows conceit: this conceit is of one kind—namely, [the conceit] "I am."
Whatever inflation of the mind there is:
this conceit is twofold—
conceit consisting in self-exaltation and conceit consisting in disparaging others …pe…
This is conceit in its tenfold form:
here someone generates conceit on account of birth, or clan, or ... or on account of some other basis; he knows and sees [this].
This is full understanding through knowledge (ñātapariññā).
What is the full understanding by scrutinization?
Having made this known, one scrutinizes conceit as impermanent, as suffering ... [and so on] ...
one scrutinizes it as an escape. This is the full understanding by scrutinization.
This is the full understanding through investigation.
What is the full understanding through abandoning?
Having thus investigated, one abandons conceit, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease to exist.
This is full understanding as abandoning.
"And he should fully understand conceit" means: he should fully understand conceit by means of these three kinds of full understanding—thus, "and he should fully understand conceit."
One should live abstaining from rashness.
What is rash conduct?
The conduct of one who is lustful, characterized by passion, is rash conduct.
For one who is corrupt, there is the conduct of hatred and the conduct of recklessness;
for one who is deluded, there is the conduct of delusion and the conduct of recklessness;
for one who is bound, there is the conduct of conceit and the conduct of recklessness.
For one who has clung [to views], there is the conduct of dogmatic views and the conduct of recklessness;
for one who has fallen into distraction, there is the conduct of restlessness and the conduct of recklessness;
for one who has gone to what is undesirable, there is the conduct of doubt and the conduct of recklessness.
The habitual conduct of one who has become firmly established in latent tendencies is "reckless conduct"— this is reckless conduct.
One who lives refraining from reckless conduct, who is aloof from reckless conduct, detached, abstinent, fully withdrawn, and escaped from it.
"May he dwell, move, wander, conduct himself, behave, protect, preserve, and maintain himself with a mind that is completely liberated, detached, and free from boundaries—
he should live abstaining from violence."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One should not be led away by the transgression of lying;
one should not form attachment to forms.”
One should fully understand conceit and live free from rashness;
one should not delight in the past.
One should not practice patience toward a newcomer;
one should not grieve when falling behind,
nor should one be dependent on space.
"One should not delight in what is old":
"What is old" refers to past form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One should not delight in, praise, or exult over past formations by way of craving or by way of views.

"New" refers to present form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

One should not, by way of craving or by way of views, form an approval toward these present formations; one should not form a desire, one should not form an affection, one should not form a lust; one should not produce it, should not generate it, should not bring it about, should not cause it to arise.

When almsfood...
when lodgings...
when medicinal requisites for the sick are diminishing, decreasing, falling away, becoming deficient, and disappearing.
"When it is vanishing, one should not grieve, nor be distressed, nor cling, nor lament, nor wail with a broken heart,
nor fall into confusion"— this means that when it is declining,
one should not grieve.
"One should not be attached to space.
Here, "space" refers to craving—that which is lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
For what reason is craving called "space"?
Because by means of that craving one draws toward, draws out, grasps, clings to, and adheres to form; [and likewise] feeling... [and so forth].
perception … volitional formations … consciousness …
the destiny … the rebirth … the rebirth-linking …
One draws toward existence… toward saṃsāra… toward the round; one pulls it together, grasps it, clings to it, and adheres to it.
Because of that, craving is called "space.
"One should not be attached to space" means one should not be dependent on craving.

"One should abandon craving, dispel it, bring it to an end, and lead it to non-existence; one should be detached from craving, abstain from it, refrain from it, have emerged from it, be escaped from it, and be liberated from it; one should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries"—thus one would not be dependent on space.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
One should not delight in the old,
nor take pleasure in the new;
one should not grieve when things decline.
One should not be attached to space.
I call greed the great flood;
I call craving the rushing current.
The object causes trembling;
the mire of sensual desire is hard to cross over.
Greed, I say, is the great flood.
Greed is said to be craving.
That which is lust, infatuation … [as before] … covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
The great flood is said to be craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness—that I call a "great flood.
"Greed I call a great flood" means:
I declare it, I teach it, I make it known, I establish it, I reveal it, I analyze it, I make it plain, I illuminate it.
Greed, I say, is the great flood;
craving, I say, is the urge.
By "urge" is meant craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness;
even the act of yearning is called craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
“I call craving ‘longing’; I call craving ‘longing,’ I declare, ... [and so on] ... I make plain, I reveal—it is craving I call longing.
The object is the trembling.”
Craving is also called the "object";
it is that lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
Craving is also called "trembling."
That which is lust, infatuation, ... [as far as] covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness—this is the object that causes wavering.
"The mire of sensual desire is hard to cross."

"The mire of sensual desire, the mud of sensual desire, the defilement of sensual desire, the swamp of sensual desire, the obstruction of sensual desire, which is difficult to escape, difficult to cross over, difficult to traverse, difficult to ford, difficult to transcend, difficult to pass beyond"— thus,
"the mire of sensual desire is difficult to escape. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“I call greed the great flood;
I call longing the rushing current;
the object of perception is the agitation.”
The mire of sensual desire is difficult to cross.
Having emerged from the truths, the sage—
the brahmin— stands on firm ground.
Having relinquished everything,
he is indeed called "peaceful.
The sage does not deviate from the truth.
Not swerving from truthful speech, not swerving from right view, and not swerving from the noble eightfold path—he is a sage (*muni*).
"Sage" (*muni*) means wisdom... [as before] ...having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a sage.
The sage, not overstepping the truths, stands on firm ground; he is called a brahmin.
"Firm ground" is said to be the deathless Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna—that is the Brahmin.
Because he has banished seven things, he is a Brahmin... [as it is said] ...he is unattached, such-like; he is called a Brahmā.
"The Brahmin stands on firm ground."

"He stands on firm ground, he stands on an island, he stands in a refuge, he stands in a shelter, he stands in a sanctuary, he stands in fearlessness, he stands in the unconditioned, he stands in the deathless, he stands in Nibbāna"— thus it is said,
"the brahmin stands on firm ground. He has relinquished everything.
"All" refers to the twelve sense bases:
the eye and forms ... [and so on] ...
the mind and mental phenomena.
When desire and lust for the internal and external sense bases have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump,
rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future, to this extent everything has been relinquished, vomited out, released, abandoned, and renounced.

When craving, views, and conceit have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising— then to this extent everything has been relinquished, vomited up, released, abandoned, and cast aside.
When the formative action of merit, the formative action of demerit, and the formative action of the imperturbable have been abandoned,
cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising— then to this extent everything has been relinquished.
"Vomited, urinated, abandoned, relinquished"—
having relinquished all that,
he is indeed called "peaceful."
Thus, being at peace, tranquil, stilled, extinguished, and calmed, one is said, spoken of, told, illustrated,
and designated as "one who is at peace.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
The sage has transcended all truths;
the brahmin stands on firm ground;
having relinquished everything, he dwells free from attachment.
He indeed is called "the peaceful one.
He is truly the wise one, the master of knowledge,
who, having understood the Dhamma, is independent.
Living rightly in the world,
he does not envy anyone here;
he is indeed wise, he is a master of knowledge.
One who knows is a knower, one who has reached true knowledge, one who possesses wisdom, one who is discerning, one who is intelligent.

"A master of the Vedas" (vedagu): the "Vedas" are said to be the knowledge in the four paths ... [and so on] ... one who is free from passion regarding all feelings, having transcended all that is felt, is called a "master of the Vedas."
"He indeed is the wise one, the knower of the Vedas;
having known the Dhamma as independent.
"Having known" means: having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest.
Having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and having known,
understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering" ... and that "whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation."
"Independent": there are two dependencies—the dependency of craving and the dependency of views... [as follows] ...this is the dependency of craving...
[as follows] ...
This is reliance on views.
Having abandoned reliance on craving and relinquished reliance on views, one is independent of the eye… independent of the ear…
Not dependent on the nose...

[and so on] ...not dependent on things seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; not clinging, not approaching, not adhering, not obsessed, and not intent upon them; having gone out, having escaped, being liberated, and dissociated, he dwells with a mind that has transcended all boundaries—thus, "having known the Dhamma, he is not dependent."
"He conducts himself rightly in the world": when,
regarding the internal and external sense bases, desire and lust have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and are subject to non-arising in the future— it is to this extent that he conducts himself, dwells, and moves about rightly in the world.
It turns, it protects, it sustains, it maintains...
[as before] ...when the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and are subject to non-arising in the future— to this extent, he conducts himself rightly in the world.
He dwells, moves, conducts himself, protects, maintains, and sustains himself—
thus he is one who conducts himself rightly in the world.
He does not envy anyone here.
"Longing" (pihā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
It is that which is lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
For whomsoever this longing, this craving, has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising by the fire of knowledge—
Burnt out, he has no longing for anyone— whether a kshatriya, a brahmin, a vaishya, a shudra,
a householder, one gone forth, a deva, or a human—
he has no longing for anyone here.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He indeed is the wise one, the master of knowledge,
who, having understood the Dhamma, is independent.”
“Living rightly in the world,
he does not envy anyone here.
He who has transcended the sensual pleasures here—
Attachment in the world is difficult to overcome;
he does not grieve nor long for anything,
his stream cut off and free from bonds.
Whoever has transcended sensual pleasures, which are so difficult to transcend in the world.

"Whoever" means whoever of such a kind, as one who is joined [to the world], as one who is disposed, as one who is of such a character, as one who has reached such a state, as one who is endowed with such qualities—whether a kshatriya, a brahmin, a vaisya, a sudra, a householder, a renunciant, a deva, or a human being.
"Sensual pleasures" (kāmā), in brief, are of two kinds:
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements...
[as above] ...these are called sensual pleasures as objects...
[as above] ...these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.
"Entanglements" refers to the seven entanglements:

the entanglement of lust, the entanglement of hatred, the entanglement of delusion, the entanglement of conceit, the entanglement of views, the entanglement of defilements, and the entanglement of misconduct.
"World" refers to the world of the states of misery, the world of human beings, the world of the devas, the world of the aggregates, the world of the elements, and the world of the sense bases.

Attachment in the world is difficult to transcend. He who has crossed over, gone beyond, leaped across, surmounted, transcended, and passed beyond attachment in the world— which is difficult to transcend, difficult to traverse, difficult to cross, difficult to surmount, difficult to pass beyond,
and difficult to overcome— that one here has transcended sensual desires, attachment which is difficult to transcend in the world.
"He does not grieve, he does not lament.
He does not grieve over an object that has changed, nor does he grieve when an object has changed.
"My eye has changed," he does not grieve... [and so on].
