He does not grieve.
He does not burn with fever (*nājjheti*): he does not burn, does not brood over, does not contemplate with longing, does not meditate with longing, does not brood intensely.
Alternatively, he is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear.
"He does not brood" means:
he does not grieve, he does not brood.
"With the stream cut, free from bonds."
“Stream” (sota) is a term for craving.

Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [and so on] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness—when this stream of craving has been abandoned by someone, utterly cut off, ... [and so on] ... consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called “one whose stream is severed.”
"Unbound" means: the bond of lust, the bond of hatred, the bond of delusion, the bond of conceit, the bond of views,
the bond of defilements, and the bond of misconduct— when these bonds have been abandoned, utterly cut off,
and burnt away by the fire of knowledge, he is called "unbound."
With the stream cut, he is without bonds.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"He who here has transcended sense-desires..."
Attachment in the world is difficult to overcome;
he does not grieve nor yearn,
for his stream is cut and he is free from bonds.
Dry up that which was before;
let there be nothing for you behind;
if you do not grasp at anything in between, you will not be caught.
"You shall wander in peace.
Dry up what was before. This means:

regarding past formations, whatever defilements might arise, dry them up, thoroughly dry them up, parch them, thoroughly parch them; render them seedless, abandon them, dispel them, bring them to an end, and cause them to cease to exist.
In this way too, dry up that which was before.

Or else, those past formative volitional actions whose results have not yet ripened—dry them up, thoroughly dry them up, parch them, thoroughly parch them; render them seedless, abandon them, dispel them, bring them to an end, and cause them to cease to exist.
In this way too, dry up that which was before.
"Later on, let there be nothing for you.
"Later on" refers to the future.
With reference to future formations, whatever "cluttering" (kiñcana) might arise—namely, the cluttering of lust, the cluttering of hatred, and the cluttering of delusion.
The conceit-encumbrance, the view-encumbrance, the defilement-encumbrance, and the misconduct-encumbrance:
these encumbrances, do not let them be yours; do not produce them, do not generate them, do not bring them forth, do not cause them to arise, do not cause them to be reborn;
abandon them, dispel them, bring them to an end, and lead them to non-existence.
"Let there be nothing for you afterwards;
if you will not grasp at the middle.
By "the middle" is meant the present forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness.
Regarding present formations, you will not grasp them through craving or through views;
you will not take them up, you will not cling to them, you will not delight in them, you will not pursue them, and you will not adhere to them.
You will abandon, dispel, and bring to an end delighting, welcoming, adhering, grasping, clinging, and insistence.
"You shall lead it to non-existence"—
if you do not grasp it in the middle.
"You shall wander at peace."
Because of the subsiding, the calming, the pacifying, the allaying, and the extinguishing of lust;
because of the subsiding, the calming, the pacifying, the allaying, and the extinguishing of hatred; ...
[and so on] ... because of the subsiding, the calming, the pacifying, the allaying, and the extinguishing of all unwholesome volitional formations.

Because you are extinguished, because you have departed [from defilements], because you are calmed, you will move, dwell, conduct yourself, behave, protect, maintain, and sustain yourself as one who is peaceful, tranquil, stilled, extinguished, and calmed— thus,
"you will move as one who is tranquil."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Dry up what is before you;
let there be nothing for you behind.
If you do not grasp at the middle,
you will wander in peace.
Completely regarding name-and-form,
He for whom there is nothing cherished as "mine," and who does not grieve over what is non-existent,
truly is not overcome in this world.
"Completely, in regard to name-and-form, for whom there is nothing cherished.
"Completely" (*sabbaso*) means: in every way, entirely, in all manners, without remainder, without residue; this is a term signifying total inclusion—"completely."
"Name" refers to the four formless aggregates.
"Form" refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
"Of whom" means of the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Mamāyita" (clung-to) refers to two kinds of "mine-ness":
the mine-ness of craving and the mine-ness of views... [etc.
...this is the mine-ness of craving... [etc. ...
This is the measure of views.

"In name-and-form entirely, for whom there is no 'mine-ness'" means that for whom there is no possessiveness toward name-and-form in every respect—[possessiveness] which does not exist, is not present, is not found, and is not obtained;
[possessiveness] which has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided.
"Rendered incapable of arising, burnt by the fire of knowledge"—
this refers to one for whom there is no sense of "mine" whatsoever regarding name-and-form.
And because of that non-existence, he does not grieve.
He does not grieve over a thing that has changed, nor does he grieve when a thing has changed.
He does not grieve thinking, "My eye has changed," nor [does he grieve] regarding my ear...
My nose...
my tongue...
my body...
Forms are mine… sounds are mine… odors are mine…
Tastes are mine… tangibles are mine… family is mine…
The assembly is my [support]...
the dwelling is my [support]... the gain is my [support]... pe...
“He does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion, thinking, ‘My blood relatives have changed.
Thus, he does not grieve over what is non-existent.

Or alternatively, when touched, overcome, overwhelmed, and possessed by painful feeling that is non-existent, he does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.”
Thus, even when what is non-existent does not exist, he does not grieve.
Or else, when touched and overcome by eye-disease...

[and so on] ...or touched and overcome by the contact of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things; being thus afflicted, possessed, and overwhelmed, he does not grieve, does not suffer, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.
Thus, one does not grieve over what is non-existent.

Or alternatively, when something is non-existent, unperceived, and unapprehended, one does not grieve, does not suffer, does not lament, and does not beat one's breast, thinking: "Alas, it was mine! Alas, that is no longer mine! Alas, it might have been mine! Alas, that I do not obtain!"
"He does not weep and does not fall into delusion.
Thus, he does not grieve over what is non-existent.
"He indeed is not defeated in the world."

For one who has grasped, clung to, adhered to, become obsessed with, and is intent upon any form, feeling, perception, mental formation, or consciousness— whether thinking "this is mine" or "this belongs to others"— for such a person there is affliction. For this has also been said:
“I have lost my chariot and my jeweled earrings;
I have likewise lost my children and my wife;
I have lost all my possessions without exception.”
Why do you not rejoice at a time for sorrow?
Wealth abandons a mortal first;
the mortal abandons wealth even sooner.
Those who desire sensual pleasures possess wealth that is impermanent;
therefore, I do not grieve when it is time for sorrow.
The moon rises, waxes full, and then wanes.
Having blazed forth, the sun goes to its setting;
I have understood these worldly conditions, Sattuka,
therefore I do not grieve at a time for grieving.
For one who has nothing whatsoever belonging to form, feeling, perception, volitional formations,

or consciousness that is grasped, clung to, adhered to, settled upon, or obsessed over— thinking "this is mine" or "this belongs to others"— for such a person there is no suffering. For this has also been said:
“You rejoice, ascetic?
“What have you gained, friend?
“In that case, ascetic, you must grieve.”
“What have you lost, friend?
“In that case, ascetic, you neither rejoice nor do you grieve.
“That is so, friend.”
"Ah, after such a long time,
we behold the brahmin who has attained final nibbāna—
the monk who is joyless and free from affliction."
“Having crossed over the attachment to the three worlds,” he indeed is not overcome in the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He for whom there is no sense of ‘mine’ regarding name-and-form in every respect,
and who does not grieve over what is non-existent— ”
"He indeed is not conquered in the world," [said the Blessed One],
"for whom there is no thought 'this is mine,' nor anything belonging to others."
Not finding anything to call "mine," he does not grieve, thinking, "It is not mine.
For him there is nothing that he thinks "this is mine," nor anything belonging to others.
"Of whom": of the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.

Of whom there exists nothing whatsoever—whether pertaining to form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness—that has been grasped, adhered to, settled upon, clung to, or devoted to, such that one thinks, "This is mine" or "This belongs to others.
There is nothing [of this nature] for him; it does not exist.
It is not found, it is not obtained; it has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided;
it is incapable of arising again, being burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
Thus, for one who has neither "this is mine" nor anything belonging to others, [there is no more suffering].
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, this body does not belong to you, nor does it belong to others.
Monks, this should be seen as old karma that has been performed and intended, which is now to be experienced."
In this regard, monks, the well-taught noble disciple carefully and thoroughly attends to dependent origination thus:

"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering."
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations...
Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
In this way, for one who has no sense of "this is mine," nor anything whatsoever belonging to others.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“O Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as empty.”
Having uprooted the view of self,
one may thus transcend death;
thus beholding the world, one transcends death.
“King Death does not see him.
Thus it is for one who thinks, “This is mine,” or who has no concern for anything belonging to others.
For this was also said by the Blessed One:
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it.
When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
And what, monks, is not yours?”
“Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Feeling… [and so on]”
Perception ...
volitional formations ...
consciousness are not yours; abandon them.
“Having abandoned that, it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
What do you think, monks? If people were to carry away the grass, wood, branches, and foliage in this Jeta’s Grove, or burn them, or do with them as they please, would it occur to you:
‘People are carrying us away, or burning us, or doing with us as they please’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“And why not? “Because this, venerable sir, is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.”
“In the same way, monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it.
When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
And what, monks, is not yours?
“Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Feeling …”
Perception ...
volitional formations ...
consciousness are not yours; abandon them.
"That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Thus it is said of one who thinks "this is mine," or who possesses anything belonging to others.
For this too has been spoken:
For one who sees, as it truly is, the arising of pure phenomena and the continuity of pure formations,
There is no fear, O village headman,
when one perceives with wisdom the world as being like grass and sticks.
He desires nothing else at all,
except for non-relinking [to further existence].
Thus it is for one who has no thought of "this is mine," nor anything belonging to others.
The bhikkhunī Vajirā said this to Māra the Evil One:
“Whom do you conceive of as a ‘being,’ Māra?
Have you fallen into a wrong view?”
This is merely a heap of pure formations;
no being is found here.
Just as, when the parts are assembled, [the word "chariot" arises].
Just as there is the sound "chariot," so when the aggregates exist,
there is the conventional designation "being."
For it is suffering alone that arises,
suffering that stands and passes away;
nothing other than suffering arises.
“Nothing else ceases with suffering.
Thus it is for one who thinks, “This is mine,” or who has any concern for others.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“In the same way, monks, a monk investigates form as far as the extent of form’s range;
he investigates feeling … perception …”
He investigates volitional formations … consciousness as far as the range of consciousness extends.
As he investigates form, as far as the range of form extends…
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
“By investigating consciousness as far as the range of consciousness extends—
even that which he has as ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’— that too does not exist for him.
Thus, for one who has no sense of “this is mine,” nor any concern for others whatsoever.
The Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“‘Empty is the world, empty is the world,’ it is said, Bhante.
In what way, Bhante, is it said that ‘the world is empty’?”
“But because, Ānanda, it is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, therefore the world is said to be ‘empty.
And what, Ānanda, is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self?
The eye, Ānanda, is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self.”
Forms are empty,
eye-consciousness is empty,
eye-contact is empty.
That is to say: whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too is empty;
the ear is empty;
sounds are empty.
The nose is empty;
odors are empty;
the tongue is empty.
Tastes are empty...
the body is empty...
tangibles are empty...
The mind is empty...
phenomena are empty...
mind-consciousness is empty...
“Mind-contact is empty;
that is to say, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self.
Because it is empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self, Ānanda, it is called ‘the world is empty.’”
Thus, for one who has neither "this is mine" nor anything belonging to others, there is no discovery of possessiveness.
There are two kinds of possessiveness: [possessiveness regarding the self and possessiveness regarding what belongs to others].
The intoxication of craving and the intoxication of views … [as above] … this is the intoxication of craving … [as above] … this is the intoxication of views.
Having abandoned the conceit of craving, having relinquished the conceit of views, not finding, not finding thoroughly, not attaining, and not acquiring possessiveness—
he, not finding possessiveness,
does not grieve, thinking, “It is not mine.”
He does not grieve over an object that has changed, nor does he grieve when an object has changed.
He does not grieve thinking, "My eye has changed," nor does he grieve thinking, "My ear... [and so on]."
Thinking, "My kinsman has passed away," he does not grieve, does not languish, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion;
thinking "it is not mine," he does not grieve.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He for whom there is nothing of ‘this is mine,’ nor anything belonging to others;
not finding a sense of ‘mine-ness’— ”
“‘It is not mine,’ he does not grieve.
Free from harshness, free from craving, unshaken, and equanimous toward all things;
I shall proclaim that benefit when asked, for one who is unshakable:
he is not harsh, not greedy, free from agitation, and equal toward all things.
What is envy (*niṭṭhuriya*)?
Here, someone is envious; they are jealous of, resentful of, harbor malice toward, and feel indignation at the gains, honors, respect, esteem, veneration, and offerings received by others.
Such envy, the act of envying, the state of being envious, jealousy, the act of being jealous, the state of being jealous—this is called envy.
This is called cruelty.
One for whom this cruelty has been abandoned, cut off...
[and] burnt up by the fire of knowledge, is called "non-cruel."
"Unattached" (an-anugiddha):
"Greed" (gedha) is a term for craving (taṇhā).
It is that which is lust, infatuation... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
He for whom greed has been abandoned and utterly cut off … [as before] … consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called one who is not greedy.
He is not greedy for forms,
nor for sounds … [as before] …
He is not greedy, not clinging, not infatuated, and not obsessed with things seen, heard, sensed, or cognized;
he is free from greed, devoid of greed, abandoned of greed, relinquished of greed, released from greed, has cast off greed, and has renounced greed;
he is free from passion, devoid of passion, abandoned of passion, relinquished of passion, released from passion, has cast off passion, and has renounced passion; he is desireless and extinguished.
"Become cool, experiencing happiness, he dwells with a self that has become sublime"—
this is one who is neither harsh nor greedy.
"Unshaken, he is the same toward all things."
“Ejā” is said to be craving.
That which is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness—
when this “ejā,” which is craving, has been abandoned, cut off, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge, he is called “one who is unmoving” (aneja).
Because craving has been abandoned, he is free from agitation.
He is not shaken by gain, nor is he shaken by loss; he is not shaken by fame, nor is he shaken by infamy;
he is not shaken by praise, nor is he shaken by blame; he is not shaken by pleasure, nor is he shaken by pain—he does not waver.
"It does not tremble, it does not shake, it does not quiver"—thus it is "unshaken.
"Equal toward all things": "all" refers to the twelve sense-bases.
The eye and forms... [and so on] ...the mind and mental phenomena.

When, regarding these internal and external sense bases, desire and lust have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future, he is said to be "even in every respect."
Thus, being such-like in all respects, equanimous in all respects, and indifferent in all respects—
one is unshaken and equal everywhere.
I shall proclaim this benefit when asked, O unshakable one.
When asked, questioned, requested, entreated, or propitiated, I declare these four benefits for a person who is unshakable.
That one who is not harsh, not greedy, and unmoving, who is equal in all respects—I call him such, I declare him, ... I reveal him.
It is this benefit that I declare when asked regarding the unshakable one.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Neither harsh nor greedy, unshaken,
equal toward all things;”
"I shall proclaim that benefit when asked,
O unshakable one," said the unagitated one who understands.
He has no hesitation whatsoever;
detached from all exertion,
he sees security in every respect.
"Of the one who knows, free from agitation":
agitation (*ejā*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*).
It is that which is lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
He for whom this impulse of craving has been abandoned and utterly uprooted … [and] consumed by the fire of knowledge, is called "impulse-free.
Because the impulse has been abandoned, he is impulse-free.
He does not waver in gain, nor does he waver in loss; he does not waver in fame, nor does he waver in disrepute; nor does he waver in praise … [nor in blame].
It does not waver; it does not waver even at blame, it does not waver even in pleasure, and it does not waver even in pain— it does not shake, does not tremble, does not quiver,
does not quiver violently, does not quiver all over— thus it is "of the unshakable one" (*anejassa*).
"Vijānato" means for one who knows, understands, discerns, thoroughly discerns, and penetrates.
For one who knows, understands, discerns, thoroughly discerns, and penetrates that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and [that] "all conditioned phenomena are suffering"... [and so on].
“For one who knows, understands, discerns, and penetrates: ‘Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation’—this is the penetration of the undisturbed one who discerns.
There is no conditioned state whatsoever.”
"Formations" (saṅkhārā) are said to be the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable.
When the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable have been abandoned,
cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are no longer subject to future arising— to that extent, there are no formations.
They do not exist, they are not found, they are not apprehended; they have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed;
they are incapable of arising again, burnt up by the fire of knowledge—thus there is no longer any doubt.
"He has desisted from exertion.
Exertion is said to be the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable.
Since the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable have been abandoned and their roots cut off...

When they have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising—to this extent one has desisted from what should be undertaken, abstained, refrained, turned away, escaped, and become liberated;
with a mind free from boundaries, one dwells detached. Thus it is said: "He has desisted from what should be undertaken."
“He sees security everywhere”:
lust is a source of fear, hatred is a source of fear, delusion is a source of fear... [and so on] ...the defilements are sources of fear.
Because lust, which is a source of fear, has been abandoned... [and so on] ...because the defilements, which are sources of fear, have been abandoned, he sees security everywhere.
He sees fearlessness everywhere; he sees the absence of calamity everywhere; he sees the absence of misfortune everywhere;
he sees the absence of affliction everywhere; he sees the state of being unassailed everywhere—he thus sees security in every respect.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For one who is unshakable and discerning,
there is no further conditioning.”
“Having desisted from exertion,
he sees security everywhere. Not among equals, nor among inferiors, [does he find it].
The sage does not speak in praise of superiors;
being peaceful and free from stinginess,
he neither exalts nor disparages.
(Thus said the Blessed One:
"The Sage speaks not to those who are equal, nor to those who are inferior, nor to those who are superior. "The Sage" means: [the one who has attained silence].
“Mona” is said to be knowledge … [and so on] … having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a sage (*muni*).

He does not say, speak, utter, illuminate, or express: “I am superior,” or “I am equal,” or “I am inferior”—the sage speaks neither among those who are his equals, nor among those who are lower, nor among those who are higher.
"He is peaceful, free from stinginess.
"Peaceful" means he is peaceful because of the pacification and calming of greed;
[and] of hatred... [and so on].

Because of the stilling, the calming, the subsiding, the extinction, the extinguishing, the disappearance, and the tranquillization of delusion— and of all unwholesome volitional formations— one is peaceful, stilled, calmed, extinguished, and tranquillized; thus one is "peaceful."
"Thus, one who is free from stinginess":

there are five kinds of stinginess—stinginess regarding dwelling, [stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gain, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma]. Clinging is called stinginess.
He for whom this stinginess has been abandoned, utterly cut off, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called "one who is free from stinginess."

Free from stinginess, having cast out stinginess, having vomited out stinginess, having released stinginess, having abandoned stinginess, having relinquished stinginess—he is one who is peaceful and free from stinginess.
He neither takes up nor casts away; thus says the Blessed One.
It does not sound; thus, form is not taken up, not clung to, not grasped, not misapprehended, and not adhered to;
feeling … perception … [is likewise].
Volitional formations … consciousness … destiny …
rebirth...
relinking...
existence...
One does not take up, does not cling to, does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to saṃsāra— the round of existence— thus one "does not take."
"He does not reject" means he does not abandon, does not dispel, does not bring to an end, and does not cause the non-existence of form;
[he does not reject] feeling... perception... [and so on].
Volitional formations … consciousness … destiny …
rebirth … relinking … existence …
He does not abandon, dispel, bring to an end, or cause the cessation of saṃsāra … the round of existence.
“Bhagavā” is a designation for veneration … [and so on] … it is a realization-designation, namely, “Bhagavā.”
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"The Sage does not speak among equals, nor among inferiors, nor among superiors."
He is holy, free from stinginess;
he neither grasps nor rejects.
(Thus said the Blessed One.)
The fifteenth instruction: the Discourse on the Staff of Self.
